content: The International Code of Conduct on the Distribution and Use of Pesticides: Guidelines on Data Requirements for the Registration of Pesticides was published in January 2013. The Inter-Organisation Programme for the Sound Management of Chemicals (IOMC) was established in 1995 following recommendations from the 1992 UN Conference on Environment and Development. Its purpose is to enhance international cooperation and coordination in chemical safety. Participating organizations include the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the International Labour Organization (ILO), the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO), the United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR), and the World Health Organization (WHO). The World Bank and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) act as observers. The IOMC aims to coordinate the policies and activities of its participating organizations to achieve sound chemical management, focusing on human health and environmental protection. This publication was developed within the IOMC framework, but its content does not necessarily reflect the views or policies of individual IOMC organizations. The designations and material presentation do not imply any opinion from FAO or WHO regarding the legal status of any country, territory, or area, nor do they endorse specific companies or products over others of a similar nature. The material is distributed without warranty, and the responsibility for its interpretation and use lies with the reader. FAO and WHO are not liable for damages arising from its use. The views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent those of FAO or WHO. FAO and WHO encourage the reproduction and dissemination of this material for non-commercial purposes, provided the source is fully acknowledged. However, reproduction for resale or commercial purposes requires prior written permission from the copyright holders and may incur fees. The guidelines outline the scientific data and information required for governments to evaluate pesticides for registration. The guidelines also aim to facilitate data generation and application submission for pesticide registration, guide countries in determining appropriate data requirements, and harmonize data requirements for pesticide registration. The guidelines do not address data requirements for the registration of biological control agents, such as predators, parasitoids, and microbial pest control agents. Different sectors have distinct responsibilities regarding data generation, identification of data requirements, and ensuring the quality and authenticity of data supporting pesticide registration and re-registration. These responsibilities are outlined in the Code of Conduct. Governments are encouraged to introduce legislation for pesticide registration, including procedures prohibiting the sale and use of unregistered pesticides. Effective monitoring and enforcement mechanisms, such as licensing and inspection schemes for importers and retailers, should also be established. Registration criteria should consider local circumstances, social and economic conditions, literacy levels, climatic conditions, and the availability of appropriate and affordable pesticide application and protective equipment. The guidelines emphasize the importance of transparency and information exchange among responsible authorities during the pesticide registration process to avoid duplication of efforts and minimize the use of test animals. Governments should facilitate such exchanges and use publicly available, peer-reviewed data when considering registration applications. Mutual acceptance of data and recognition of registrations within regional harmonized systems should be encouraged, but registration in the country of origin should not be a requirement unless mutual recognition is sought. The guidelines were prepared in accordance with Article 6 of the International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management and under the FAO/WHO Guidelines for the Registration of Pesticides. They provide detailed recommendations on the data required to support pesticide registration, covering aspects such as product identity, composition, physical and chemical properties, risks to human health and the environment, and product efficacy. A tiered approach to data requirements is recommended, allowing for stepwise assessments based on the pesticide and its proposed uses. The guidelines also address special situations, such as biological pest control agents, emergency approvals, and experimental use. Annexes provide comprehensive lists of recommended data requirements, which are based on those required by advanced regulatory authorities in countries like Canada, the European Union, and the United States. While the requirements are extensive, member states may tailor them to their specific needs and resources. Data requirements for pesticide registration should cover all relevant aspects of the product, from manufacture to use and ultimate disposal. This includes information on the proposed application, product identity and composition, risks to humans and the environment, and product efficacy. For pesticides used on food and feed crops, applicants should provide residue data generated in accordance with Codex Alimentarius guidelines and other international standards. Residue assessments may not always require local trials; data from similar crops grown under comparable conditions in other countries may suffice. FAO and WHO recommend using maximum residue limits (MRLs) defined by Codex Alimentarius when applicable. National authorities should collaborate to set MRLs for situations not covered by Codex.
